hook.text: A cell that records its own history — CRISPR-based molecular recorders write cellular events into DNA in real time.

buildup.text: CAMERA systems use CRISPR to insert new DNA sequences when triggered — each event adds a barcode to the genome.

discovery.text: MEMOIR records gene expression history in single cells — reading the DNA reveals what genes were active and when.

twist.text: Recording capacity is limited — cells can only accumulate so many mutations before genome stability is compromised.

climax.text: Molecular recording in gut bacteria could monitor digestive health continuously — a living diagnostic inside your body.

punchline.text: DNA as a diary — molecular recorders let cells document their own lives.

quiz.question: How do CRISPR-based molecular recorders store information?
options: They store data in RNA molecules that are secreted from the cell
They insert new DNA sequences into the genome each time a cellular event triggers the CRISPR system
They change the color of fluorescent proteins to indicate different events

details.summary: Molecular recording devices use engineered biological systems to write cellular events into DNA, creating permanent records of gene expression, environmental exposures, and signaling events. CRISPR-based recorders can log sequential events in a cell's history over time.
details.whyItMatters: Cells experience countless molecular events we cannot observe in real time. Molecular recorders create a biological black box that scientists can read later, revealing hidden histories of development, disease progression, and immune responses at
takeaways: CRISPR-based systems write cellular events as permanent DNA modifications
Recorders capture the order of events, not just their occurrence
Applications include tracking tumor evolution and immune response histories

faq.question: How can cells record their own history in DNA?
faq.answer: CRISPR-based recorders use guide RNAs activated by specific cellular events to make targeted insertions in a DNA array. Each event adds a unique mark. The order of insertions can be read by sequencing, reconstructing the timeline of cellular events after the fact.

faq.question: What could molecular recorders reveal about cancer?
faq.answer: By reading a tumor cell's molecular record, researchers could reconstruct the sequence of mutations and environmental exposures that drove progression. This would reveal which events are causes versus consequences and identify the critical early events to target therapeutically.
